newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens fete rebel Basayev to mark independence.
newsitem.headline: Chechens fete rebel Basayev to mark independence.

text.p: Crowds of Chechens marked the fifth anniversary of their self-proclaimed independence a day early on Thursday, feting local rebel hero Shamil Basayev, a key figure in the struggle for freedom from Moscow.
Many in the crowd hugged and kissed Basayev, leader of a bloody raid on the Russian town of Budennovsk last year and guest of honour at the anniversary party in his home town of Vedeno.

The separatist leadership of the mainly Moslem Caucasian region proclaimed its secession on September 6, 1991. Just over three years later, an exasperated Russian President Boris Yeltsin sent in the army to bring them to heel.
After 21 months of war and tens of thousands of deaths, the two sides agreed a peace last week, postponing the question of independence for five years.
Vedeno's celebrations, held in view of mountains that were until recently topped by Russian artillery, included traditional Chechen singing, arm-wrestling, boxing, football and wrestling.
Local people streamed from villages all around southeastern Chechnya to a sports field behind Vedeno's school, many carrying the green flag of Ichkeria, the separatist name for the region.

Last June, the bearded Basayev led a small band of comrades through a string of Russian checkpoints to penetrate 70 km (45 miles) out of Chechnya and hold hundreds of people hostage in a hospital at Budennovsk.
Scores of people were killed during the assault and in the ensuing six-day standoff with Russian forces, but Basayev returned a hero to his mountainous homeland.
He also led the rebels in an attack on the capital Grozny on August 6 in which they humiliated Russian forces and seized much of the city, sparking the worst fighting in more than a year.
In Vedeno, any spirit of triumphalism was absent after a fight that seemed to many to have been won by the Chechens.
"There will only be victory when the question of power relations are solved," Basayev told reporters as he leaned on crutches to support a leg injury suffered in the Grozny battle.
"If there is enough common sense to solve this question on the basis of international standards of rights it will be a victory for both sides."
But Basayev was unshakeable on the question of Chechen independence which was at the heart of the war. "Relations have to be on the basis of two independent states," he said.
Thursday's party took place as Alexander Lebed, the Kremlin peace envoy who secured the peace deal, was holding more talks with rebel commander Aslan Maskhadov.
Basayev doubted if Lebed's deal had truly ended the war. "I will believe it when all the Russian troops have gone," he said.
Chechen fighters sauntered everywhere in Vedeno, automatic rifles and grenade launchers slung over their shoulders. But the only bangs were those of firecrackers set off by children.

People sat before a stage fashioned from a cart. Behind them a game of soccer began. Groups of elderly men sang traditional Chechen songs, mixtures of prayers and heroic ballads sung mournfully at times, picking up in warlike chants at others.
"We have come here today for a celebration where young people will show their strength, skills and readiness to fight," Basayev told the crowd.
Ruslan Maskhadov, preparing to take part in the wrestling competition, said: "No one here talks about victory...We just stood up for our independence."
